newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Seven thousand march to mourn Dutch blaze victims.
newsitem.headline: Seven thousand march to mourn Dutch blaze victims.

text.p: Seven thousand mourners marched through the Hague on Friday to the house in which a Turkish woman and five of her children died in a suspected racist arson attack.
The Hague's mayor and Dutch Development Aid Minister Jan Pronk accompanied the "march of grief and despair" through the Schilderswijk district to the burned-out shell of the Kosedag family's home.
The woman's husband and their five other children escaped from the fire on Tuesday night by jumping from an upstairs window.

The mayor earlier told relatives of the victims that the fire was apparently deliberately started, Dutch media said, though he emphasised in a television interview that it was still unclear who was responsible or what their motives were.
Media reports of a possible racist motive focused on petrol bomb attacks on the same night on nearby buildings housing an Azerbaijani-Turkish centre and a Turkish islamic association.

Police refused to comment on any possible link. Five men arrested on Thursday over the two petrol bomb attacks have now been released and are not suspects in the deadly house fire, the Hague public prosecutor said.

"(They)...were held on suspicion of throwing molotov cocktails at two cultural centres/coffee houses in the area. The prosecutor has decided to let (them) go, because they all have a firm alibi and could not have been involved," the prosecutor's office said in a statement.

Around 3,000 mourners wept and prayed in a city square earlier as the coffins of the six victims, which were draped in Turkish flags, were passed over the heads of the crowd. They were being flown to Turkey for burial on Saturday.

"This is a deeply sad neighbourhood and there is a very great deal of emotion in this city," Pronk told Dutch NOS television news. "I hope that the decency which the people of the Hague, of all colours, have shown today will continue to prevail."

Dutch Foreign Minister Hans van Mierlo sent a letter of condolence to the Turkish ambassador expressing his sympathy to bereaved relatives and his dismay that the fire appeared to have been intentionally started, the Foreign Ministry said.
"I find it very grieving that this can happen here in the Netherlands," an elderly Dutch man at the march told NOS.
"I knew the family. I have no words," a Dutch woman said.
Prime Minister Wim Kok told reporters late on Thursday that even the suspicion of a racist attack was worrying for the country, which prides itself on the tolerance of its society.
"The thought that we could be dealing with arson with some ethnic intention is dramatic. That would be an entirely new phenomenon in the Netherlands and a serious signal," he said.

A local Turkish journalist told NOS the Turkish community was shocked and confused. "The first day they were just so shocked and I was too. I thought that can't be true. That can't be true in the Netherlands," he said.
